newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: WINTER DIVING IN PORTUGAL: cold but clear.
newsitem.headline: WINTER DIVING IN PORTUGAL: cold but clear.

text.p: Portugal's Atlantic coast is at its best in the winter for sports divers who aren't afraid of the cold and who savour the rich variety of flora and fauna to be found in its clear waters.

"The visibility is clearer in the winter," says Pieter van Etten, a Dutch veteran diver who runs the Ilhas Martinhas diving centre in Sagres, a rocky outcrop on the western edge of the Algarve, the site of some of Portugal's best diving.

He said visibility reached up to 30 metres (98 feet) in the winter, giving divers a clear view of the valleys and rock gardens that hide spider crabs, lobsters and octopus and serve as the habitat for myriad fish.
The best diving is off the west coast where divers, if they are lucky, come across a sand shark, a grouper or a moray eel.
Travellers to the islands of the Azores, Berlenga and Farilhoes arguably have the best diving of all and report sightings of manta rays and whales.
Bream, bass and white compass jellyfish, which drift aimlessly with the currents, are commonplace off the Portuguese coast. So are schools of squid and cuttle-fish.

Divers descend upon gardens of greens, yellows, reds and orange, abounding in starfish, spiky anenomes, curly black sea cucumbers and shells. Sometimes, depending on the time of year, they weave their way in and out of forests of kelp.
SUMMER ALGAE
Off the fishing village of Sesimbra south of Lisbon, a popular haunt for the capital's divers, algae build up in the summer and cloud visibility.
A dive in September can be like descending into pea soup if you're unlucky.
But in the winter the algae have gone.

"The problem with the winter is that, although the diving is good, we can't promise tourists that we can dive every day because of high waves sometimes and storms," said Elmar Vees, a German who runs Blue Ocean Divers outside Lagos in the Algarve.

Joao Cabrita, a partner with Atlantic Scuba Diving in nearby Albufeira, said recently: "In the winter we can't guarantee the weather. Today it is fantastic. But today there is no one to take out. It's a chicken and egg situation."
In the winter the Portuguese Atlantic can drop in temperature to 15 degrees Celsius (59.00 Fahrenheit) at the surface from around 22 (71.60 Fahrenheit) in the summer.
Some dive centres offer dry suits that keep out the water, but most just provide rubber wet suits, which trap a thin layer of water between the diver's skin and the suit.
Diving regulars, who wear thick 7 mm longjohns, jackets, hoods and boots in the summer Atlantic, are advised to snuggle into a 3 mm vest as well in the winter.
Once properly equipped, the cold is hardly noticeable and divers are more concerned about whether an Atlantic storm is going to cause the day's boat outing to be called off.
The foreign tourists who visit Portugal's commercial diving centres in the winter, encouraged by cheap flights off season, come mainly from Britain, Germany, Scandinavia and Spain.
DIVING CENTRES
The number of foreign divers visiting Portugal in the winter has increased in recent years as diving centres upgraded their facilities and advertised in magazines and travel agencies.
Portugal's diving centres offer courses for beginners, including night dives, and some train the physically handicapped.
Most centres provide motorised inflatable boats, permitting divers to reach choice dive sites quickly.

With their weight belts fitted to ensure neutral buoyancy, divers do a backwards somersault into the sea. The boatman hands them their air tanks which they slip onto their backs before signalling to their buddy that they are ready to go down.
Divers must bring their licences and a valid medical certificate to show that they are fit to dive.
